title: When Our Parents Grow Old: A Bible Study for Caregivers
subtitle: A five-session study on honor, weariness, hard choices, and dying well, for those caring for an aging parent or an ailing husband or wife.
summary:
This study is for adult children caring for aging parents, near or far, for husbands and wives caring for a spouse whose body or mind is failing, and for the churches that should not leave them alone. Its five sessions take up what the command to honor father and mother asks of grown children; the weariness no one sees, with Elijah under the broom tree; the reversal of roles, through Ruth and Naomi and Jesus entrusting his mother to the disciple he loved; the hard choices about where a parent will live, money, siblings, and a parent who was not a good parent; and dying well and grieving, with a plain account of hospice and palliative care. Each session is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation, and each ends in prayer rather than advice.

This guide is not medical, legal, or financial advice. It says plainly that caregiver exhaustion and depression are real, that elder abuse and neglect happen, sometimes at the hands of family, and that safety comes first. A caregiver with thoughts of suicide should call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, now. So should a caregiver afraid of hurting the person they care for, after making sure that person is safe and stepping away; no one has to be suicidal to call. Anyone who suspects an older adult is being harmed, neglected, or exploited should report it to adult protective services, and call 911 if anyone is in danger.

The study refuses two easy answers: that honor means doing it all yourself, and that grown children owe their parents only what they choose to give. Scripture commands honor as something weighty and done in deeds, sets rest beside it, and gives the burden to a family and a church rather than to one exhausted son or daughter. Where faithful Christians differ, the study states each view fairly and leaves the question open. And it implicates the church, which has too often prayed for the sick by name and forgotten the people who bathe them.
audience: Adult children caring for aging parents, spouses caring for a husband or wife, and the churches around them

sessions.title: Honor in a New Season
sessions.aim: To read the command to honor father and mother where Scripture sets it, beside the command to rest, and to learn from Jesus' rebuke of Corban and from 1 Timothy 5 that honor is weight carried in deeds and shared by many hands.
sessions.summary:
Most of us learned the command to honor our father and mother as children, when it sounded like a rule about doing what we were told. It was spoken at Sinai to grown men and women, and many of us only discover its weight in middle age. Two answers compete. The voice of duty says honor means doing it all yourself, for as long as it takes, and it is right that the command binds. The voice of freedom says grown children owe their parents only what they choose to give, and it is right that honor never requires anyone to stand within reach of abuse. Alone, the first crushes caregivers and the second abandons parents.

Scripture holds what neither voice can. The Hebrew word for honor comes from a root meaning heavy, and the command stands right beside the command to rest. Jesus condemned a religious loophole that let a son walk away from his parents (Mark 7:9-13), and 1 Timothy 5 asks families to "repay their parents" (1 Timothy 5:4) while the church cares for those who have no one. Honor is heavy, and it was never meant to be carried by one person, or carried without rest.

keyScripture.why: "Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you" (Exodus 20:12). Spoken at Sinai to a whole people, adults included, it comes directly after the command to rest (Exodus 20:8-11), a rest for everyone in the household.

discussion.q: Before tonight, what did you think the command to honor your father and mother asked of you as an adult? Who taught you, and has caring for an aging parent changed your answer?
discussion.behind: Surface the defaults before teaching anything. Some learned the command as a rule about obedience, some heard it used as a weapon, and some had a parent it is painful to think about honoring. Don't correct anyone yet. Spouses can answer about their own parents or their in-laws. Anyone may pass; go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Exodus 20:8-12 aloud. The command to honor parents comes right after the command to rest, a rest given to everyone in the household. What do you make of those two commands standing side by side?
discussion.behind: Let the room notice the neighbor before you explain it; Leviticus 19:3 puts the two commands in one verse. Watch for two misreadings: the exhausted caregiver who hears one more rule to fail, and the person who hears permission to step back from a parent. The text is neither; it is a word from the God who knows what honoring costs.

discussion.q: Read Mark 7:9-13. What was the Corban tradition, and why was Jesus so angry about it? What respectable reasons might we use today to set aside what we owe our parents?
discussion.behind: Explain the practice simply: a son could declare what his parents would have received from him devoted to God, and the tradition then held him to the vow, so that he was no longer permitted to help them. Let the room find modern versions: a schedule full of good things, church things included, a career that can't bend. Keep it self-implicating, and protect caregivers who already give more than they have; the passage is aimed at walking away, not at their exhaustion.

discussion.q: Read 1 Timothy 5:3-8 and 16. Who is asked to do what? What changes when you see that the family and the church each carry a share?
discussion.behind: Verse 8 is often aimed like a missile at people already worn out, so read it in its place: a letter that comes in Paul's name, about widows in a world without pensions. Families provide for their own, and the church cares for "the widows who are truly in need" (1 Timothy 5:16). Then ask the church members present what share they have taken.

discussion.q: Where have you leaned toward the voice of duty or the voice of freedom with your own parents? What has it cost you, or them?
discussion.behind: Move from the text to the self, gently. Some have tried to do everything and are breaking; some have kept a careful distance and feel the guilt of it. Go first, briefly. If someone's answer touches a parent who was harsh, absent, or abusive, thank them, don't ask for details, and say that the fourth session takes that up.

objections.objection: Honor means doing it yourself. My mother cared for her own mother at home until the end. Anything less is putting my comfort ahead of the people who raised me.
objections.response: Honor what is true here. Caring for a parent at home is costly love, often given out of sight, and Jesus condemned the tradition that let a son walk away. But Scripture never names the method or the address, and it sets honor beside rest. Where a parent should live is a question faithful Christians answer differently, and the fourth session takes it up. Doing all of it yourself is another matter. When Moses tried to settle every dispute in Israel himself, his father-in-law told him, "the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone" (Exodus 18:18). Even at home, the care can be shared with brothers and sisters, friends, the church, and paid help. You are already giving yourself. The harder question is whether you will let others give too, because a caregiver who breaks has nothing left to give.

objections.objection: Grown children don't owe their parents anything. We didn't ask to be born. Talk of honor is just a religious way to guilt people into years of unpaid care.
objections.response: Concede what is true. Duty preached without help has crushed people, and some parents did harm no one should be shamed into standing near again. But the objection pictures life as a set of contracts we chose, and many of the weightiest things in a life were never chosen. Nobody chooses their parents, and nobody chooses to need help in the bathroom at eighty-five. Scripture's honor is not a bill for services rendered. It recognizes that your father and mother are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27) and did not lose their worth when they lost their usefulness. The same faith protects the caregiver: it commands rest, calls the church to share the load, and never asks anyone to call harm love. It explains, better than a contract can, why anyone keeps visiting a mother who no longer knows who came.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What would honoring your parent look like this week if you did not have to do all of it yourself?
sessions.practice: This week, write down three things honor could mean for your parent now, in deeds rather than feelings: a meal, a call to the doctor's office, an hour listening to a story you have heard before. Beside them, write one way you will rest. If your parent lives far away, choose one act of provision you can do from where you are. If you are carrying more than you can bear, tell one person the whole truth. Read Exodus 20:8-12 each morning. For a companion between sessions, the eight-week plan at /plans/caregiving takes these weeks one small practice at a time.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you gave us parents we did not choose, and you commanded us to honor them. Some of us have honored them gladly, some through clenched teeth, and some from a distance, for reasons only you fully know. Forgive us where we have walked away, and where we have tried to carry what you never asked one person to carry. Where something was broken long before this, heal what can be healed, and keep safe those who must honor from a distance. Thank you for setting rest beside honor, and for your Son, who even on the cross made sure his mother was cared for. Teach us to treat our fathers and mothers as weighty, and to let others help. In Jesus' name. Amen.
reflection: What did I learn growing up about what I owe my parents, and has it helped or hurt me now?
Where am I tempted to set aside what I owe my parent for reasons that sound respectable, and where am I trying to carry what was never meant for one person?
What would it mean for me to honor my parent and to rest, both in the same week?
sessions.teaching:
Most of us learned this command as children, when it sounded like a rule about doing what we were told. At Sinai, though, God spoke it to a whole people, grown men and women included: "Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you" (Exodus 20:12). The letter to the Ephesians calls it "the first commandment with a promise" (Ephesians 6:2). The Hebrew verb translated honor comes from a root meaning heavy. To honor your parents is to treat them as weighty, as people who still count. That is why honor is not the same as obedience, and why it outlasts a parent's strength and even a parent's memory. A mother who no longer knows your name still carries weight before God.

When a parent begins to decline, two voices start to speak, and both deserve a hearing. The voice of duty says honor means doing it yourself, all of it, without complaint, for as long as it takes. Scripture supports more of this than its critics allow: the command binds, and the Bible expects provision in deeds, not only warm feelings. The voice of freedom says grown children owe their parents only what they choose to give, and that a caregiver's life matters too. It also has truth on its side. Honor was never meant to be slavery, a caregiver's limits are real, and no one is required to stand within reach of a parent who harms them. Spoken alone, each does damage. Duty alone produces exhausted caregivers who are ashamed to ask for help. Freedom alone produces parents who are visited at Christmas and otherwise left to strangers, or to no one.

Scripture refuses both, beginning with the command's neighbor. Immediately before it stands the command to rest, "Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy" (Exodus 20:8), a rest for the whole household, servants and foreigners included. When Deuteronomy repeats it, it spells out one reason: "so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do" (Deuteronomy 5:14). Leviticus puts the two in a single verse: "Each of you must respect his mother and father, and you must keep My Sabbaths" (Leviticus 19:3). The God who told you to honor your father and mother also told you to stop. Honor carried without rest is not a more faithful version of the command. It is a different command from the one God gave.

Then look at what Jesus did with the command. Pharisees and scribes had criticized his disciples for eating without the ritual washing their tradition required, and Jesus turned the charge around. Their tradition let a man tell his father or mother, "Whatever you would have received from me is Corban" (Mark 7:11), a gift devoted to God, and after that "he is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother" (Mark 7:12). Jesus answered, "Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down" (Mark 7:13). Honor includes provision, not only respect. And the loophole Jesus condemned was a religious one, which let a man look devout while his parents went without. Those of us who lead churches should hear that first, because a congregation can make it easier to be at church than at a parent's bedside, and I'm a pastor, so that warning includes me.

The same pattern runs through 1 Timothy 5, a letter that comes in Paul's name to Timothy in Ephesus, in a passage about widows in a world without pensions. Children and grandchildren "must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God" (1 Timothy 5:4). Then comes the sentence people aim like a missile: "If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever" (1 Timothy 5:8). Read in its place, it rebukes people who walk away. It was never written for the daughter who has provided for years and can't do it alone anymore. Nor does the passage stop with the family. A believer with widows in her family is to help them and not burden the church, "so that it can help the widows who are truly in need" (1 Timothy 5:16), the ones left with no one. Family and church each carry a share.

So why does honor so often feel like one person's private burden? Partly because many of us live scattered across states, in households that depend on two incomes, and partly because of the church. We pray for the sick by name and forget to ask who is bathing them, and we admire the caregiver from a distance and assume someone else is helping. Honor is heavy, and God meant it to be. He also set rest beside it, and in the New Testament he told his church to share the load, which is the part that falls to the rest of us. Many of you already honor your parents at a cost no one has counted. Whether you go on carrying it alone is a question for everyone else in this room.

scriptureStudy.note: "Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy" (Exodus 20:8), and four verses later, "Honor your father and mother" (Exodus 20:12). The command to honor comes straight after a rest given to everyone in the household. Honor and rest were given together.

"Each of you must respect his mother and father, and you must keep My Sabbaths." The two commands share one verse. Later the same chapter says, "You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God" (Leviticus 19:32), tying respect for the old to the fear of God.

"You neatly set aside the command of God to maintain your own tradition" (Mark 7:9). The Corban vow let a son devote to God what his parents would have received from him and then refuse to help them. Jesus treats provision for parents as part of the command.

"If anyone does not provide for his own ... he has denied the faith" (1 Timothy 5:8). The warning is for those who walk away, not for those worn out from staying. Verse 16 asks families to help their own so that the church can help "the widows who are truly in need."

"Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old." The proverb names the season this study is about. Contempt for the old can grow quietly in a tired heart, and the wisdom of Israel names it before it hardens.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up what honor has meant in practice, because the long tradition behind the command treats it as concrete work, not a sentiment. A teaching preserved in the Babylonian Talmud (Kiddushin 31b) defines honoring a parent in plain terms: giving food and drink, clothing and covering, and helping them come and go. The earliest church was just as concrete about its widows. When the Greek-speaking widows in Jerusalem "were being overlooked in the daily distribution of food" (Acts 6:1), the apostles had the church choose seven men "full of the Spirit and wisdom" (Acts 6:3) to see that no one was missed. In the sixth century the Rule of Saint Benedict told monks to treat the old with kindly consideration, mindful of their weakness.

Set that beside the account the sociologist Robert Bellah and his colleagues gave in Habits of the Heart (1985). They argued that individualism had become the first language of American moral life, with the biblical and civic traditions surviving as second languages. In the first language, a good life is independent and chosen, and needing help looks like failure. It struggles to explain why anyone should keep visiting a parent who can no longer give anything back. A serious group should ask which language it speaks when a parent declines, and what it would take for a church to speak the older one again as a practice of shared care.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose two people speak in the first session. A man in his fifties says his mother cared for her own mother at home for years, so he has moved his father into the spare room. He works full time, his wife sleeps on the couch so she can hear the old man at night, and last week his father was found in the street at two in the morning. He says he will never put his father in a home. Across the circle, a woman whose parents live in another state says quietly that she feels like a fraud, because all she can do is call on Sundays and pay for a helper twice a week.

Don't settle it for either of them. Read Exodus 20:8-12 and John 19:25-27, and ask the room what honor is asking of each, and what rest would look like in his house. Afterward, speak privately with him about his father's safety: a parent found wandering at night is a reason to call the doctor right away, and in an emergency, 911. Use this to show that honor takes different shapes at different distances, and that wherever a parent lives, no one household was meant to carry the care alone.

sessions.title: The Weariness No One Sees
sessions.aim: To name the hidden exhaustion of caregiving and the resentment and guilt inside it, and to read Elijah under the broom tree and Galatians 6 as God's answer of sleep, bread, presence, and shared burdens, without treating a caregiver's limits as failure or a caregiver's despair as small.
sessions.summary:
The weariness of caring for an aging parent, or for a husband or wife whose health is failing, is built from things that happen out of sight, and under it there are often feelings no one says out loud: resentment toward a parent for needing so much, guilt for resenting people you love, and sometimes a wish that it were all over. The usual advice pulls two ways. Some say love doesn't count the cost, so pray harder and stop complaining, and they're right that love is costly. Others say to put yourself first, because you can't care for anyone after you collapse, and they're right that limits are real. Taken alone, the first advice shames the caregiver and the second leaves them alone with their own resources.

Scripture answers differently. When Elijah sat down under a broom tree and asked to die, God let him sleep, fed him, touched him, and did it all twice. And Paul told the churches of Galatia, "Carry one another's burdens" (Galatians 6:2). Scripture meets a caregiver's exhaustion with bread, rest, and other people.

keyScripture.why: Elijah "sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die" (1 Kings 19:4), and God answered with sleep, bread, water, and a touch, then came back to do it again: "Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you" (1 Kings 19:7). God's first answer to a servant with nothing left is care for his body, not a rebuke.

discussion.q: What part of caring for your parent, or your husband or wife, does no one else see? If you aren't a caregiver, what have you noticed, or missed, in someone who is?
discussion.behind: Let people name it concretely: the nights, the bathroom, the paperwork, the repeated questions, the quiet house. Naming turns a vague guilt into a list of real work. Don't hurry to comfort or solve anything yet. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read 1 Kings 19:1-8. Elijah has just come from a great victory, and now he asks to die. What does God do for him, and what does God not do?
discussion.behind: Help the room see the order: God lets Elijah sleep, feeds him, touches him, and comes back a second time, and the questions come later. Caregivers are often given advice when they need bread. If anyone says Elijah's prayer has been theirs, thank them, don't explore it in the group, and talk with them privately as soon as the session ends, following the leader's primer.

discussion.q: Many caregivers resent the people they love and then feel guilty for resenting them. Read Psalm 13:1-2 and Ephesians 4:26. What is the difference between feeling resentment and letting it rule?
discussion.behind: Feeling resentful isn't automatically sin; it is often a warning light that the load is too heavy or that someone isn't helping. The psalm brings complaint straight to God, and the letter to the Ephesians says, "Be angry, yet do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26). The danger is in keeping it: contempt, taking it out on the parent, or quietly withdrawing care. Let people say what they're ashamed of without anyone rushing to correct them.

discussion.q: Read Galatians 6:2-5 and 9-10. Which part of what you carry is the heavy kind of burden others should help with, and who has never been asked?
discussion.behind: Paul uses one word for the heavy burden of verse 2 and another for the pack each person carries in verse 5, and a parent's decline is the first kind. Verse 9 is spoken to a community carrying together, not as a whip for one person carrying alone. Press for names; many caregivers know people who offered help in general and have never been asked for something specific.

discussion.q: Where have we, as a church and as friends, let someone carry this alone? What would it take to notice the caregiver as well as the patient?
discussion.behind: Turn the mirror inward, starting with yourself. Let the room make one concrete commitment before it leaves: a meal, an afternoon, a ride, a visit to the parent. Keep this from becoming a guilt session. The point is to act.

objections.objection: Love doesn't count the cost. If I'm tired and resentful, it's because I'm selfish. I should pray harder and stop complaining.
objections.response: Take this seriously, because it usually comes from someone who loves hard. Love is costly, and complaint can curdle. But look at how God treats his tired servants. Elijah asked to die, and God sent bread. Moses said he could not carry the people by himself, and God gave him seventy elders to share the burden (Numbers 11:14-17). Paul told the Corinthians that he and his companions had been "under a burden far beyond our ability to endure" (2 Corinthians 1:8), and that God delivered them (2 Corinthians 1:10). Each of them reached the end of his strength, and each time God answered with help. "For He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). Your exhaustion is not proof that you are selfish. It may be proof that you are carrying what was meant for many, and it may also be something your doctor should hear about.

objections.objection: The answer is self-care. You have to put yourself first, because you can't pour from an empty cup.
objections.response: Grant what is right. Rest is commanded, a caregiver's health matters, and one who collapses can't help anyone. Jesus himself told his tired disciples, "Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while" (Mark 6:31). But notice the difference. The language of self-care leaves you alone with your own resources and turns rest into one more task you are failing at. In Scripture rest comes as a gift, and help comes from other people: Jethro, the seventy elders, the angel with the bread, a church told to carry burdens. And your parent still needs care while you rest, so the question that matters most is who else will take a share and make rest possible at all.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If someone offered to take one thing off your list this week, what would you hand them, and what would keep you from saying yes?
sessions.practice: This week, keep one list of whatever the care took each day: the rides, the pills, the calls, the nights. By the end of the week, choose one item and ask one specific person to take it, with a day and a time, such as sitting with your father on Thursday afternoon. If they say no, ask someone else. Each night, do one plain kindness for your own body. If you are afraid you might hurt your parent, or your thoughts turn toward ending your own life, make sure everyone is safe, step away, and call or text 988 now. If you aren't a caregiver, offer one specific help to someone who is, and do it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you know our frame, and you remember that we are dust. Some of us are more tired than we have told anyone, and ashamed of what the tiredness has done to our hearts: the resentment, the short temper, the wish that it would end. We bring it to you because you can bear it. Do for us what you did for Elijah: let us sleep, feed us, touch us, and come back again. Send people to share what we cannot carry, and give us the humility to let them. Forgive your church for every caregiver we have left alone. Carry the ones we carry, and carry us. Amen.
reflection: What has this care cost me that I have not admitted to anyone, God included?
Where has resentment been a warning light in me, and where has it started to rule?
Who could take one burden from me this week, and what keeps me from asking?
sessions.teaching:
People ask how your mother is doing, and few think to ask about you. The weariness of caregiving is made of things that happen out of sight: the pill organizer refilled on Sunday night, the third trip to the bathroom at two in the morning, the same question asked before lunch and again after it. If you care for a husband or wife, there is a particular loneliness inside it, a marriage in which one of you has become the nurse. Under the tiredness there are often feelings no one says out loud: resentment toward your parent for needing so much, toward a brother or sister who calls with opinions and rarely comes, and sometimes toward God. Then comes guilt for resenting people you love, and for the moment you caught yourself wishing it were over. The second weight is often heavier than the first.

Two answers are usually offered. The first is duty: love doesn't count the cost, so pray harder and complain less. Love is costly, Christ gave himself, and complaint can curdle into bitterness, so this answer has Scripture on its side. But spoken alone it teaches caregivers to hide their exhaustion until it breaks them. The second is self-care: put yourself first, because you can't care for anyone if you collapse. Limits are real and rest is commanded, so this answer has truth in it too. Yet on its own it leaves the caregiver alone with their own resources, turns rest into one more assignment, and says nothing about who will care for the parent while the caregiver rests.

Scripture tells a story that answers both. Elijah had just stood against the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. Then Queen Jezebel swore to kill him, and he ran. He left his servant at Beersheba, went on alone into the wilderness, and "sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die. 'I have had enough, LORD,' he said. 'Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers'" (1 Kings 19:4). Scripture doesn't hide that the great prophet had nothing left, and neither should we. Caregivers sometimes reach that place too. If you are there tonight, I would rather you tell someone and call or text 988 than read another line.

Then watch what God does. He doesn't rebuke Elijah or remind him of the fire on Carmel. He lets him sleep. An angel touches him and says, "Get up and eat" (1 Kings 19:5), and there is bread baked over hot coals and a jar of water. Elijah eats and lies down again, and the angel comes back, touches him again, and says, "Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you" (1 Kings 19:7). God's first answer to a servant with nothing left is sleep, food, and touch, twice. The questions come later, at Horeb, where Elijah pours out the voice of isolation: "I am the only one left" (1 Kings 19:10). God answers that, too, with something better than an argument. He gives Elijah work to do, a companion and successor in Elisha, and the news that he was never as alone as he felt: "I have reserved seven thousand in Israel" (1 Kings 19:18).

The pattern runs through Scripture. When Moses tried to settle every dispute in Israel by himself, his father-in-law told him, "You cannot handle it alone" (Exodus 18:18). Later Moses told God, "I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me" (Numbers 11:14), and God took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and put it on seventy elders, so that "They will help you bear the burden of the people, so that you do not have to bear it by yourself" (Numbers 11:17). Paul made the pattern a way of life for the churches of Galatia: "Carry one another's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). A few lines later he says, "For each one should carry his own load" (Galatians 6:5), with a different word, the pack each person carries for himself; a parent's long decline is the heavy kind of burden. Then he writes, "Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). That sentence has been used as a whip on people carrying alone. It was written to a community that carried burdens together, and the next verse tells it to do good "especially to the family of faith" (Galatians 6:10). The caregiver in the third pew is in the family of faith.

What about the resentment? Feeling it isn't automatically sin. It is often a warning light that the load is too heavy, that someone who should help isn't helping, or that an old wound has opened, and the psalms give you words to bring it to God: "How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day?" (Psalm 13:2). The danger is in keeping it, nursing it into contempt, taking it out on your parent, or letting it harden into a quiet withdrawal of care. And know when the weariness has become something more: when you've stopped sleeping or eating, can't stop crying or feel nothing at all, or are drinking more to get through the evening. See your own doctor and say you're a caregiver. If you have begun to think everyone would be better off without you, or you are afraid you might hurt your parent or yourself, make sure everyone is safe, step away, and call or text 988 now; you don't have to be suicidal to call.

We have to stand inside this. Caregivers can quietly disappear from worship because they can't leave a parent alone, and the rest of us can mistake their absence for drifting. If you are this tired, the scandal is less your exhaustion than how easily the rest of us let it happen. The angel brought Elijah bread, and then came back with more.

scriptureStudy.note: "Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you" (1 Kings 19:7). God's first answer is bodily: sleep, bread, water, and a touch, then all of it a second time. Elijah went on "strengthened by that food" (1 Kings 19:8).

"I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well" (1 Kings 19:10). Isolation tells Elijah he is alone. God answers with a still, small voice, new work, a companion and successor in Elisha, and the news that thousands in Israel have stayed faithful.

"I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me" (Numbers 11:14). God answers Moses' limit by sharing the Spirit with seventy elders, who "will help you bear the burden of the people" (Numbers 11:17).

"Carry one another's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2). Paul uses one word for the heavy burden others help carry and another for the load each person carries himself (Galatians 6:5). A parent's decline is the heavy kind.

"Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). Spoken to a community carrying burdens together, it is encouragement, not a whip, and the next verse points the good work "especially to the family of faith" (Galatians 6:10).

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the church's older wisdom about carrying one another, which is wiser than either the voice of duty or the voice of self-care. In Life Together, written in 1938 and published in 1939, Dietrich Bonhoeffer called the law of Christ in Galatians 6:2 a law of bearing. He argued that other Christians are not only people we enjoy but people we must bear, weaknesses and all, and that it is precisely when another person becomes a burden to us that we learn what it means to have a brother or sister, because God bore our burden in Christ. He was writing about Christian community, not caregiving, but caregivers know the truth of it from the inside.

The Rule of Saint Benedict, from the sixth century, is more practical still. It tells monks to care for the sick before and above everything else, serving them as Christ himself, who said, "I was sick and you looked after Me" (Matthew 25:36). It asks the sick not to distress those who serve them with excessive demands, asks the servers to bear patiently with the sick all the same, and makes the abbot responsible for seeing that no one is neglected. A serious group should ask what a congregation would have to change to become that kind of circle for its caregivers.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in his seventies has cared for his wife since a stroke three years ago. In the second session he says, almost cheerfully, that he's fine and the Lord gives him strength. At the break he mentions that he hasn't slept through the night in months, that their children live far away, and that last week he shouted at his wife when she spilled her breakfast, then sat in the car and cried.

You will want to tell him anyone would have done the same, or to quote him a verse about strength. Do neither. Thank him for telling you. Ask him privately whether he is afraid he might lose control again or hurt her, and whether he has had thoughts of harming himself; if so, make sure his wife is safe, stay with him, and call or text 988 together, and if anyone is in danger, call 911. Then help him think about rest: who could sit with his wife for an afternoon, and whether her doctor or a social worker knows how tired he is. Use the scenario, never a real person's private words, to show the room that the cheerful answer is often the loneliest one.

memoryVerse.text: Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

sessions.title: When Roles Reverse
sessions.aim: To read Ruth and Naomi, an old man named Barzillai, and Jesus' care for his mother from the cross as pictures of love that changes shape when the one who once cared now needs care, and to weigh a parent's dignity and wishes against safety without letting either swallow the other.
sessions.summary:
There is a moment many adult children remember: the first time they helped a parent with something the parent used to do for them, cutting meat or buttoning a coat. Spouses know their own version. Two instincts pull against each other, and both are love. Protection says a declining parent can't always judge what is safe, so decide for them, and safety does matter. Respect says it is their life, so honor their wishes, and overriding an adult can humiliate. Protection without respect turns a parent into a problem to be managed, and respect without protection can leave a parent in danger.

The book of Ruth tells of a young widow who refused to leave her bitter mother-in-law, worked to feed her, and saw her restored, and it ends with Naomi holding a grandson on her lap and becoming his nurse. When an old man who had provided for King David asked to die in his own town, David honored the wish. And Jesus, dying, gave his mother into the keeping of the disciple he loved. In each story love changes its shape and keeps its object.

keyScripture.why: "For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16). Ruth binds herself to a bitter, grieving older woman who has tried three times to send her away, and the book shows the promise kept until Naomi's life is renewed.

discussion.q: When did you first realize you had become the one taking care of your parent, or of your husband or wife? What did that moment feel like?
discussion.behind: Let people tell the moment: a fall, a bill left unpaid, a wrong turn on a familiar road, a doctor talking to them instead of the patient. Many feel grief and awkwardness at once, and spouses may describe losing a partner who is still there. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Ruth 1:8-18. Naomi tries three times to send Ruth away. Why might an older person push away the help they need, and what do you notice about the way Ruth stays?
discussion.behind: Naomi has buried a husband and two sons, believes she is too old to start over, and thinks God is against her. Aging parents push help away out of grief, pride, fear of being a burden, or a disease that has changed them. Ruth's vow was freely chosen hesed, devotion beyond duty, so no caregiver should hear it as a demand to promise everything; and she had help from Israel's harvest law and a generous relative.

discussion.q: Read 2 Samuel 19:31-39. Barzillai turns down the king's offer to live at his side. How does David respond, and where are your parent's wishes in tension with what you think is best?
discussion.behind: Notice Barzillai's fear of becoming "an added burden" (2 Samuel 19:35), and his wish to die in his own town. David honors the choice and blesses him. Let the room name their own tensions. Then name the hard edge: when a parent's choices endanger the parent or others, love may have to say no, with a doctor's help and with the parent's voice in it.

discussion.q: Read John 19:25-27. While he was dying, Jesus arranged care for his mother. What did he do himself, and what did he entrust to someone else?
discussion.behind: Jesus couldn't take his mother home, so he gave her into the keeping of the disciple he loved, who took her in "from that hour" (John 19:27). Arranging care is not walking away. For adult children far away this is a word of permission; for those nearby, a picture of a shared household. Leave care facilities for the next session.

discussion.q: At the end of Ruth, Naomi becomes a nurse to her grandson. How could you help your parent keep giving and not only receiving? And what frightens you about needing care yourself someday?
discussion.behind: Naomi's restoration came partly through being given someone to care for. Parents can keep giving in small ways: a story told, advice asked for, a prayer for the grandchildren. Then turn the question inward. Many of us fear depending on others more than we fear death, and that fear shapes how we treat a parent who depends on us. Go first.

objections.objection: It's her life. If my mother wants to stay in her own house and drive her own car, I have no right to take that away from her.
objections.response: Start with what is true. Your mother is an adult made in the image of God, and her wishes deserve weight; the command to honor does not make grown children their parents' rulers, and taking decisions from someone who can still make them humiliates. Barzillai chose where he would die, and the king honored it. But love doesn't ignore danger. When a parent's choices endanger the parent or someone else, a driver who can no longer judge distance or a stove left burning, honor may require a hard no. Make that decision with a doctor's assessment, with your mother's voice in it as far as possible, and with whatever legal authority your state requires; an elder law attorney can tell you what applies, and this is not legal advice.

objections.objection: My father can't make good decisions anymore. It's easier and kinder to decide for him and not upset him with the details.
objections.response: Grant the love in this, and the realism. Some decisions really are beyond a parent with advanced dementia, and sparing someone needless worry can be a kindness. But easier for whom? Even people with serious memory loss can often say what they want to eat, whom they want to see, and what frightens them, and asking honors them. Deciding everything without them teaches them they no longer count, and the command to honor says they do. Ask what you can, explain what you can, and decide only what you must.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What do you think your parent is most afraid of losing, and have you ever asked them?
sessions.practice: This week, have one conversation with your parent that isn't about logistics. Ask what matters most to them now, or about something they remember, and listen without steering toward a decision. If your parent can no longer hold a conversation, sit with them, hold a hand, play music they love, and let the hour count. Write down one way your parent could keep giving. If you care for a husband or wife, choose one thing that still belongs to the two of you as husband and wife, not patient and nurse, and protect it. Read Ruth 1 aloud once this week.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you carried us from the womb, and you promised to carry your people to old age and gray hair. Now some of us are carrying the ones who carried us, and we don't know how. Give us Ruth's loyalty without her loneliness, and give our parents Naomi's restoration after her bitterness. Teach us to honor their wishes and to protect them from harm, and give us wisdom when we can't do both. Thank you for your Son, who from the cross made sure his mother had a home. And when our own strength fails, carry us too. Amen.
reflection: When I help my parent, do I tend to take over or to look away, and what fear is underneath it?
What wish of my parent's have I brushed aside, and what wish have I honored that put them at risk?
What would it take for me to accept care someday without believing I had lost my worth?
sessions.teaching:
There is a moment many adult children remember: the first time you cut your father's meat, or buttoned your mother's coat, or sat in a doctor's office while the doctor spoke to you instead of to her. Spouses have their own version, the day a husband became the patient and his wife the nurse. The roles reverse, and no one prepared either of you for it. The parent may resist help, hide a fall, or insist on driving. The caregiver may swing between treating a parent like a child and pretending nothing has changed.

Two instincts pull against each other, and both are love. Protection says a declining parent can't always judge what is safe, so decide for them, and a parent who wanders at night or drives through red lights really is in danger. Respect says it is their life, so honor their wishes, and overriding an adult who can still decide really is a humiliation. Protection with no respect turns a parent into a problem to be managed, and respect with no protection can leave a parent alone with a danger they can no longer see.

The book of Ruth, set in the days when the judges ruled, is the story of an older woman whose life collapsed. Famine drove Naomi and her husband from Bethlehem to Moab, where her husband died and then both her sons. Turning home, she tried three times to send her widowed daughters-in-law back to their families. She was too old, she said, and "the hand of the LORD has gone out against me" (Ruth 1:13). Ruth would not go: "For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16). In Bethlehem, with Ruth standing beside her, Naomi told the women of the town, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty" (Ruth 1:20-21). Grief can make an older person unable to see the love in front of them, and Ruth kept giving it anyway.

Ruth's loyalty has a Hebrew name, hesed, loving devotion beyond what duty requires, and it took the plainest forms. She gleaned in the barley fields, and at day's end she "brought out what she had saved from her meal and gave it to Naomi" (Ruth 2:18). Someone noticed: "I have been made fully aware of all you have done for your mother-in-law," Boaz told her (Ruth 2:11). Nor did Ruth carry Naomi alone. Israel's law left the gleanings "for the poor and the foreigner" (Leviticus 19:10), so one woman's loyalty worked inside a provision Israel's farmers were commanded to keep. At the end, the women of Bethlehem say Ruth's son "will renew your life and sustain you in your old age" (Ruth 4:15), and "Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him" (Ruth 4:16). The woman who had been cared for became a caregiver again. Older people keep their dignity partly by continuing to give, and a wise caregiver looks for ways to let them.

Another old man shows what it looks like to honor a person's own wishes. Barzillai, eighty years old and wealthy, had provided for King David during Absalom's revolt. When David offered him a place at his side in Jerusalem, he declined: "Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voice of singing men and women? Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?" (2 Samuel 19:35). He asked to go home, "that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother" (2 Samuel 19:37). David did not argue. He took Chimham in Barzillai's place, as the old man asked, and "The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home" (2 Samuel 19:39).

Not every wish can be honored safely. Jesus told Peter, "when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go" (John 21:18). John explains that Jesus meant the death Peter would die (John 21:19), so the verse is not about aging, but its picture describes what many families live. A day may come when love has to lead a parent out of the driver's seat, or into a place with help at night. Decide it with a doctor's assessment, with as much of your parent's voice as possible, and with whatever legal authority your parent's state requires; none of this is legal advice.

Then stand at the cross. Mary stood near it, and Jesus, in agony, saw her and the disciple he loved, whom Christians have long identified as John. He said to her, "Woman, here is your son," and to the disciple, "Here is your mother" (John 19:26-27). "So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home" (John 19:27). The Son who could no longer care for his mother with his own hands made sure she would be cared for. The roles had reversed in the most terrible way, and he honored her anyway.

Underneath all of this is a fear most of us share, the fear of needing help. In the language of independence, a parent who needs help feels like a burden, Barzillai's own word, and a caregiver who struggles feels like a failure. Scripture speaks another language. Every person bears the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and that image does not leave when strength or memory does. We all began life carried, and God promises his people, "Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray" (Isaiah 46:4). If you care for a husband or wife, you may have made a promise for this without imagining it: the marriage vow many English-speaking Christians have spoken, which reached us through the Book of Common Prayer of 1549, promises love in sickness and in health until death. Love changes its shape when a parent or a spouse declines. It does not change its object.

scriptureStudy.note: "Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried" (Ruth 1:17). Ruth's vow reaches to death and burial. It is freely given hesed, and no caregiver should hear it as a demand to promise more than they can give.

"I have been made fully aware of all you have done for your mother-in-law" (Ruth 2:11). Someone saw the unseen work and prayed for God to repay it. Ruth fed Naomi from her own portion (Ruth 2:18), under Israel's harvest law, which left grain for the poor and the foreigner.

"And Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him" (Ruth 4:16). The book ends with the cared-for becoming a caregiver again. Naomi's restoration came through being given someone to love.

"Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?" (2 Samuel 19:35). Barzillai declines the king's generosity and asks to die in his own town, and David honors the choice. An old person's wishes carry weight.

"I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you" (Isaiah 46:4). The passage sets idols that must be carried, "a load to the weary animal" (Isaiah 46:1), beside the LORD who carries his people from birth to gray hair.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up one of the hardest questions caregivers face when a parent's memory fails, because faithful Christians answer it differently. A father with dementia asks every evening where his wife is, though she died three years ago. Told the truth, he grieves her as if for the first time; told she is out at the store, he settles. Some Christians hold that the truth is still owed, since Scripture says, "each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor" (Ephesians 4:25), and a confused father is still a neighbor made in God's image. Truth can be gentle: you can answer the longing under the question and turn the conversation without saying anything false. Their comfort is a clear conscience and a parent never treated as less than a person.

Other Christians hold that when a disease has taken the ability to hold a painful truth, entering a parent's confused world to spare him fresh grief is not the lie Scripture forbids. The commandment forbids false witness against a neighbor (Exodus 20:16), and "Love does no wrong to its neighbor" (Romans 13:10). Their comfort is that a caregiver need not make a father grieve his wife's death afresh every evening. Both agree that deceiving a parent for anyone's gain is wrong. The guide leaves the question open, and so should the group. Underneath it lies what Christians on both sides affirm: a person's worth before God does not depend on memory. When Zion complained that the Lord had forgotten her, God answered by imagining a mother forgetting her own child: "Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!" (Isaiah 49:15).
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group says her father, a widower in his eighties, still drives himself to church and the store. Twice this month he has come home with a dent he can't explain, and a neighbor saw him drive through a stop sign. When she raised it, he said taking his keys would be the end of his life. Her brother, in another state, tells her to leave him alone.

Don't tell her to take the keys tonight, and don't side with her brother. Read 2 Samuel 19:34-39 and Romans 13:8-10, and ask the room what honoring her father's dignity looks like, and what loving him, and the strangers on the road, requires. Then help her think about a next step that keeps his voice in it: asking his doctor to assess his driving, bringing her brother into the conversation, and planning other rides to church and the store, so that losing the keys doesn't mean losing his world. Safety and dignity are both forms of honor.

memoryVerse.text: Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.

sessions.title: Hard Choices
sessions.aim: To face the decisions a parent's decline brings, about housing, money, siblings, and a parent who was not a good parent, with Scripture's wisdom and the counsel of others, leaving open what faithful Christians leave open and never asking anyone to stand within reach of harm.
sessions.summary:
Sooner or later the decisions come, and they rarely wait for a good moment: where Mom will live now, who will pay for the help she needs, who will sign the papers, why one sibling carries nearly everything while others help little, or help from far away. For some there is a harder question still: what honor means toward a father or mother who was harsh, absent, or cruel. These are rarely choices between right and wrong. More often they are choices between two kinds of loss, made under pressure by tired people.

Scripture gives no floor plan, but it gives wisdom. It shows David, a fugitive with nowhere safe for his parents, asking the king of Moab to shelter them (1 Samuel 22:3-4). And it holds the command to honor beside the plain fact that some parents did real harm, refusing to let honor mean pretending or a return to danger. Where faithful Christians differ, the session states both views and leaves the question open. Nothing in it is legal or financial advice. Its counsel is the one Scripture gives again and again: ask God for wisdom, and don't decide alone.

keyScripture.why: Fleeing from Saul, with no safe place for his parents, David asked the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me" (1 Samuel 22:3), and "he left them in the care of the king of Moab" (1 Samuel 22:4). Arranging care through someone else is not walking away.

discussion.q: What decision about your parent's care are you facing now, or dreading? Who is in the room when it gets made?
discussion.behind: Let people name the actual decisions: where a parent will live, driving, money, who can sign, whether to call hospice. Then notice who is missing from the room; many caregivers decide alone, at night, after a crisis. Don't advise anyone on a particular decision.

discussion.q: Read 1 Samuel 22:1-4 and John 19:26-27. Both David and Jesus arranged care for a parent through someone else. What is the difference between arranging care through other hands and walking away?
discussion.behind: Arranged care stays involved: it visits, asks questions, and advocates; walking away stops looking. Then set out the open question without tilting it: some believe honor leans toward home care as long as it can be done, others that a good facility, chosen with care and visited faithfully, can be honor. Both put safety first. Protect anyone who has already chosen from feeling judged.

discussion.q: Read Luke 12:13-15 and Proverbs 28:24. Where have you seen money, or the fear of it, shape a family's decisions about an aging parent?
discussion.behind: Help the room see two dangers: treating a parent's money as one's own, and letting fear of the cost decide what care a parent receives. Commend keeping records and sharing them with siblings. If anyone suspects someone is taking a parent's money, adult protective services is the place to call. Nothing here is financial or legal advice.

discussion.q: Read Galatians 6:2-5, then Genesis 25:8-9 and 35:29, where brothers who had long lived apart buried their father together. What would it take for your family to share the care, and what will you do if a brother or sister won't?
discussion.behind: Brothers who had lived apart, one pair once bitter enemies, stood together at a father's grave; that is a picture, not a promise. Think practically: a family meeting, someone neutral to lead it if old fights take over, specific requests, a written plan. If a sibling still refuses, grieve it, stop waiting, and build help elsewhere.

discussion.q: The command to honor has no exception written into it, yet a psalm that bears David's name prays, "Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me" (Psalm 27:10). If a parent was harsh, absent, or cruel, what can honor mean that requires neither pretending nor a return to harm?
discussion.behind: Say first that no one needs to share their story. Honoring a parent never means putting yourself back within reach of harm, and it doesn't require trust, closeness, or pretending the past didn't happen. Some give care with firm limits; others arrange care through someone else and check on it from a distance. If anyone discloses abuse, past or present, don't explore it in the group; thank them and talk privately afterward.

objections.objection: Putting your parent in a nursing home is abandoning them. Good families take care of their own.
objections.response: This is one of the questions on which faithful Christians differ, so state both views the way their defenders would. Some believe honor leans toward caring for a parent at home as long as it can be done; children are told to "repay their parents" (1 Timothy 5:4), and daily, costly presence is a gift no one else can give, seen by God in every hidden hour. Others believe honor can be given through other hands: when a parent's needs outgrow what a family can safely give, a good facility, chosen with care and visited faithfully, is one way to provide, and a task "too heavy for you" should be shared (Exodus 18:18). A painful decision, they would say, is not a sinful one. Both agree that abandonment is never honor and that safety comes first, the parent's and the caregiver's. Your pastor can help you weigh it.

objections.objection: My father never honored me. Why should I honor him now? After what he did, the command can't mean I owe him anything.
objections.response: The wound is real, and Scripture takes it seriously: the letter to the Ephesians, right after repeating the command to honor, tells fathers, "do not provoke your children to wrath" (Ephesians 6:4). The command to honor has no exception written into it, but honor is not what the objection fears. It is not obedience, trust, closeness, or a pretense that the past didn't happen, and forgiving someone is not the same as making yourself available to them. Honoring a parent never means putting yourself back within reach of harm. For some it looks like giving care with firm limits around it; for others, like making sure care is given by someone else, checking on it from a distance, and refusing to repay evil for evil. A counselor who understands abuse can help you see which is wise. If you are afraid of him now, get safe first.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which decision in front of you feels like a betrayal whichever way you choose, and who could help you weigh it?
sessions.practice: This week, make one call that opens a door: set a date for a family meeting, ask your parent's doctor for a social worker, or ask an elder law attorney about a durable power of attorney and a health care proxy while your parent can still understand and sign them. Write down anything your parent has told you about their wishes, and if your parent can still talk, ask. If the parent you care for was hard to love, choose one limit that makes the care survivable and keep it. None of this is legal or financial advice. The care page at /help/caregiving lists the calls that open doors.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of wisdom, you promise to give it generously to all who ask, and we are asking. We stand in front of choices we never wanted to make: where our parents will live, how the bills will be paid, what to do with brothers and sisters who help too little or too loudly. Some of us are trying to honor a father or mother who did not honor us. Keep us from walking away, and from walking back into harm. Guard our families from greed and old rivalries, and give us counselors. Where every choice means loss, help us choose in love and trust you with the rest. Amen.
reflection: What decision have I been putting off, and what am I afraid it will say about me?
Where has money, or fear about money, shaped the way I see my parent's care?
If my parent was hard to love, what can I honestly give without stepping back within reach of harm, and who could help me see that line?
sessions.teaching:
Sooner or later the decisions come, and they rarely wait for a good moment. They arrive after a fall, in an emergency room at two in the morning, or in a call from a neighbor who found Dad confused in the yard, and they are rarely choices between right and wrong; more often they are choices between two kinds of loss. Scripture gives no floor plan, but it gives wisdom and an invitation to ask for more: "Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him" (James 1:5). Proverbs adds, "Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22). So ask God, and don't decide alone. A doctor, a social worker, an elder law attorney, your pastor, and your family will see more together than one exhausted caregiver at midnight. Nothing in this guide is legal or financial advice.

Take the decision about where a parent will live, because it carries more guilt than almost any other. Scripture commands honor and provision and never names the place, and faithful Christians weigh this differently. Some believe honor leans toward caring for a parent at home as long as it can be done; children are told to "repay their parents" (1 Timothy 5:4), and daily, costly presence is a gift no one else can give. Others believe honor can be given through other hands; when a parent's needs outgrow what a family can safely give, a good facility, chosen with care and visited faithfully, is one way to provide, and a painful decision is not a sinful one. This study doesn't settle the question, and neither should your group. Both views share a floor: abandonment is never honor, and safety comes first.

Scripture does give two pictures to carry into that decision. Running from King Saul, with nowhere safe to keep his aging parents, David asked the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me" (1 Samuel 22:3). The text doesn't say why Moab, though readers of the whole Bible remember that David's great-grandmother Ruth came from there (Ruth 4:17). And at the cross Jesus gave his mother into the keeping of the disciple he loved. Neither walked away; each arranged care he could not give with his own hands. If your parent moves into a facility, honor continues in visits, questions, and advocacy, and every state has a long-term care ombudsman who advocates for residents.

Then there is money, which can poison a family's conversations as a parent declines. A man once asked Jesus, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me" (Luke 12:13), and Jesus refused to referee and warned instead, "Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed" (Luke 12:15). Proverbs is blunter: "He who robs his father or mother, saying, 'It is not wrong,' is a companion to the man who destroys" (Proverbs 28:24). Taking an older person's money is a form of elder abuse, and family members are among those who do it. A parent's savings exist first for the parent's care. Keep records, share them with your siblings, and if you suspect someone is taking your parent's money, report it to adult protective services. Medicare doesn't cover long-term custodial care when that is the only care a person needs; Medicaid may, for those who qualify in their state.

In many families one person carries nearly everything, usually whoever lives closest, while others help little or second-guess from a distance. The one far away often carries a guilt of their own, and distance is not the same as not caring. A parent's decline is the heavy burden others are told to help carry (Galatians 6:2), and a family meeting can turn vague guilt into specific shares, including ones a sibling can carry from far away: the bills, the insurance calls, money, a week's visit so the nearby caregiver can rest. If a brother or sister still refuses, grieve it honestly, stop waiting, and build help elsewhere. And notice two quiet sentences in Genesis. When Abraham died, "His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him" (Genesis 25:9), brothers separated since boyhood. When Isaac died, "his sons Esau and Jacob buried him" (Genesis 35:29), though Esau had once planned to kill his brother as soon as their father was gone (Genesis 27:41). A parent's death does not always heal a family, but sometimes it brings brothers to the same grave, and a family can pray for that without demanding it.

Then the hardest question, which some in this room carry and may never say aloud: what does honor mean toward a parent who was harsh, absent, or cruel? The command has no exception written into it, but Scripture does not pretend that parents can't fail their children. The letter to the Ephesians repeats it and in the next breath tells fathers, "do not provoke your children to wrath" (Ephesians 6:4), and a psalm that bears David's name prays, "Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me" (Psalm 27:10). Honor means treating someone as weighty. It is not obedience, or trust that was never earned, or pretending the past didn't happen. When Joseph's brothers feared his revenge after their father died, Joseph, by then a ruler in Egypt whom they could no longer harm, named their wrong without shrinking it, "As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good" (Genesis 50:20), and refused to repay it. Forgiving someone is not the same as making yourself available to them, and honoring a parent never means putting yourself back within reach of harm. Some adult children give care with firm limits; others arrange care through someone else and check on it from a distance. A counselor who understands abuse can help you see which is wise. If you are afraid of the parent you care for, or of anyone in the house, get safe first.

The church has not always helped. We have preached the command to honor father and mother as though it settled every family's choices, told people wounded by their parents to honor them without asking what happened in that house, admired the family that kept a parent at home without offering to help, and been quicker to judge the family that chose a facility than to visit the mother who lives there. Whatever a family decides, the church owes it the same thing afterward: people who keep visiting.

scriptureStudy.note: "Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me" (1 Samuel 22:3). A fugitive son arranges safety for his parents with a foreign king. Arranging care through others, when you cannot give it yourself, is a form of honor.

"Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him" (James 1:5). The letter of James sets this promise among "trials of many kinds" (James 1:2). God does not scold the one who asks for help deciding.

"Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me" (Luke 12:13). Jesus refuses to be the family's referee and warns against "every form of greed" (Luke 12:15). A parent's decline can bring greed to the surface, and Jesus names it.

"Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me." In a psalm that bears David's name, the LORD receives the one whom parents have failed. An adult child let down by a parent can still turn to a Father who does not let go.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the long history behind these choices, because the guilt many carry about care facilities rests partly on a picture of the past that is too simple. In Scripture, care for the old happens in households that are not left alone: Ruth gleaned in fields the law required farmers to leave unstripped, and the widows of 1 Timothy 5 were the shared concern of families and the church. When the church in Jerusalem found widows overlooked, it organized their care (Acts 6:1-4). Through the Middle Ages, monasteries and church-founded hospitals and almshouses took in the sick, the poor, and the old who had no one. The nursing homes, assisted living residences, and home care agencies families weigh today took their present shape in the twentieth century, and Medicare and Medicaid, created in 1965, shaped how that care is paid for.

None of that settles what any family should do. It does mean the choice is not between a golden past in which every family cared for its own and a cold present that hands parents to strangers. A serious group should ask what it would take for a congregation to be present where its older members now live: visiting the nursing home, learning the aides' names, noticing who has no visitors.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group has cared for her widowed mother for four years. Her mother's memory is failing, she has fallen twice this year, and the doctor says she should not live alone. The woman's brother, two states away, sends money every month and is convinced their mother would be lost in a facility; he wants more help brought into the house instead. Her younger sister hasn't spoken to their mother in years, for reasons the family has never discussed. The woman says she is exhausted and angry at both of them, and ashamed of being angry.

Don't tell her what to do about her mother, and don't take sides between the siblings. Read Galatians 6:2-5 and Proverbs 15:22, and ask the room what a fair share might look like for each sibling and who could help lead a family meeting. Remind the room that faithful Christians differ about home and facility care, and that both views put safety first. Say gently that the younger sister owes no one an explanation for her distance. Afterward, ask the woman privately how she is sleeping.

memoryVerse.text: Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.

sessions.title: Dying Well and Grieving
sessions.aim: To face the end of a parent's or a spouse's life honestly, with Psalm 71 and 2 Corinthians 4 as companions, to understand in general terms what hospice and palliative care are and are not, and to make room for the grief that begins before a death and continues after it.
sessions.summary:
Many deaths now come slowly, and the people caring for a declining parent begin grieving long before the end. Near the end come questions few families prepare for: whether to call hospice, whether to keep pursuing treatment, how to talk about dying, and what to do with the relief that sometimes comes with grief. Two failures tempt us. Denial keeps fighting at any cost and never says the word, holding on to a hope that does matter. Resignation treats the dying as already gone, having accepted a death that does come to everyone. But denial can leave the dying isolated inside a lie, and resignation can leave them alone before they are gone.

Psalm 71 is the prayer of someone old who fears being cast aside: "Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails" (Psalm 71:9). Paul wrote, "Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16), because he believed that the One who raised Jesus will raise us too. This session describes hospice and palliative care in general terms, which is not medical advice, and it leaves room for tears. Death is still an enemy. It is not the last word.

keyScripture.why: "Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails" (Psalm 71:9). The psalmist, old and gray, asks not to be forsaken "until I proclaim Your power to the next generation" (Psalm 71:18). The old still have something to give, and the God who taught them from youth does not let go of them at the end.

discussion.q: How did your family talk about death when you were growing up, if it talked about it at all? How has that shaped the conversations you are having, or avoiding, now?
discussion.behind: Most families have a habit around death: silence, euphemism, dark humor, or plain speech. Let people name theirs without judging it. The point is to see how inherited habits shape what happens at a bedside now, including the conversations that never happen. Go first.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 71:9-12 and 17-20. What does this old person fear, and what do they still hope for? How might it change your visits to pray this psalm for your parent, and then as your own?
discussion.behind: The psalmist fears being discarded and hopes to tell the next generation what God has done, so encourage people to ask for their parents' stories. Then turn the psalm around, because the caregiver's strength is failing too. If a parent can no longer speak, the psalm can be prayed aloud at the bedside.

discussion.q: What have you heard about hospice and palliative care? What fears or misunderstandings do people bring to them?
discussion.behind: Correct misunderstandings gently and generally, and say this is not medical advice. Palliative care relieves pain, symptoms, and stress at any stage of a serious illness; hospice is palliative care near the end of life for someone who has chosen comfort over cure. Neither aims to hasten death or to postpone it, hospice cares for the family too, and a person can leave it if things change. Encourage families to ask the doctor directly.

discussion.q: Read 2 Corinthians 4:7-18. Paul says the outer self is wasting away while the inner self is renewed. What does that mean beside a bed where the outer self is visibly failing, and what does it not mean?
discussion.behind: It does not mean the body doesn't matter or the loss isn't real. Paul's hope is resurrection, "the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us" (2 Corinthians 4:14). Calling affliction light is a comparison with glory, not a dismissal of pain. Don't let anyone use the passage to hurry someone's grief.

discussion.q: Many caregivers grieve long before a death, then feel relief when it comes, and guilt for the relief, or for not being there at the last moment. Read Matthew 26:36-41. What do you make of Jesus' words to friends who couldn't stay awake?
discussion.behind: Jesus asked his closest friends to keep watch with him, and they fell asleep. He named it, said "the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" (Matthew 26:41), and did not stop loving them. Relief after a long illness is not betrayal, and missing the final moment does not undo years of presence. Leave the grief unresolved.

objections.objection: Choosing hospice is giving up. If we had enough faith, we would keep fighting and keep praying for healing.
objections.response: Honor what is right in this. God heals, and the letter of James tells the sick to call the elders to pray, promising that "the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick" (James 5:15). The fear of giving up usually comes from love. But hospice is not the end of prayer or of care. It changes the aim of medical care from cure to comfort, and it aims neither to hasten death nor to postpone it. Our hope was never in the next treatment. Death is "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and Christ has already defeated it. This is not medical advice; ask the doctor, and ask your pastor.

objections.objection: Talking about death with my mother will only frighten her. It's kinder to keep her hopeful and never say the word.
objections.response: Grant the kindness. Some people don't want to talk about dying, families and cultures differ, and no one should force a conversation on a frightened person. But silence can become a lie that isolates the very person it means to protect; Tolstoy's The Death of Ivan Ilyich shows a dying man tormented most by the lie everyone around him keeps up, that he is only ill and not dying. Scripture shows another way: Jacob spoke of his death and told Joseph where he wanted to be buried, and his sons kept the promise (Genesis 47:29-31; 50:12-13). Let the dying lead. Ask what they want to know and what they want to say. You don't have to force the conversation, and you don't have to forbid it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you knew there was only a little time left, what would you want to be sure was said or done? And if the time is already gone, what do you wish you had said?
sessions.practice: This week, pray Psalm 71 slowly each day, once for your parent or spouse and once for yourself. If your parent can still talk, ask one question you would regret not asking. If a serious illness is advancing, ask the doctor plainly whether palliative care or hospice could help now. Write down what you would want if you were the one in the bed, and tell someone where to find it. If your parent or spouse has already died, let yourself grieve without a schedule; the care page at /help/grief and the plan at /plans/grief can help in the weeks ahead.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you were with our parents from their mothers' wombs, and you promised to carry your people to old age and gray hair. Do not discard them in their old age, and do not forsake them when their strength fails. Do not forsake us either; our strength is failing too. Give us courage to speak honestly with the dying and gentleness to let them lead. Where death has already come, comfort us, and keep us from grieving like people without hope. Your Son committed his spirit into your hands, and you raised him. Into your hands we commit the ones we love, and ourselves. Amen.
reflection: What conversation about death have I been avoiding, and what am I afraid would happen if I had it?
Where have I already begun to grieve someone who is still alive, and have I let anyone comfort me for it?
What do I believe about my own death, and how would I want to be cared for at the end?
sessions.teaching:
Many deaths now come slowly. A parent declines over months or years, through hospital stays and rallies and new diagnoses, and the people caring for them begin grieving long before the end. Those who care for a parent with dementia often lose them in pieces too small for anyone else to notice: the stories first, then the names, then the recognition in the eyes. There is no funeral for any of it. This is anticipatory grief, and it is real grief, not a lack of faith. When the end comes, many caregivers also feel something they are ashamed to admit, which is relief. Relief after years of watching someone suffer is not betrayal. Very often it is love that has been grieving for a long time.

Near the end, two failures tempt us. The first is denial: keep fighting at any cost, never say the word, keep everyone hopeful.
