Hope does matter, but denial can leave the dying alone inside a lie, unable to say what they need to say. The second is resignation: treat the dying as already gone, and stop visiting because she doesn't know you anyway. Death does come to all of us, and some treatments only add suffering, but resignation abandons a person before death has taken them.

Psalm 71 walks between them. It is the prayer of someone old who has trusted God since youth and now fears being set aside: "Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails" (Psalm 71:9). It also holds a purpose: "Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation, Your might to all who are to come" (Psalm 71:18). The old still have work to do, and the psalmist expects more than the grave: "You will revive me once again. Even from the depths of the earth You will bring me back up" (Psalm 71:20). Pray it for your parent, and ask for the stories while there is time. Then pray it as your own.

Scripture also shows a death spoken of and prepared for. When Jacob knew his time was near, he asked Joseph to bury him with his fathers, and Joseph promised (Genesis 47:29-31). "When Jacob had finished instructing his sons, he pulled his feet into the bed and breathed his last, and he was gathered to his people" (Genesis 49:33). Then "Joseph fell upon his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him" (Genesis 50:1), and his sons buried him where he had asked. Families can do the same: ask a parent, while they can answer, what they want at the end, put it in the written forms their state recognizes, and keep the promise.

This is where hospice and palliative care come in, and they are often misunderstood. In general terms, and not as medical or legal advice: palliative care is medical care that relieves the pain, symptoms, and stress of a serious illness, and it can begin at diagnosis, alongside treatment meant to cure. Hospice is palliative care near the end of life. In the United States it is generally offered when a doctor expects that the illness, if it runs its usual course, will end in death in six months or less, and the person chooses comfort rather than treatment aimed at cure. It is given wherever the person lives, at home, in a nursing home, or in a hospice residence, by a team that usually includes doctors, nurses, aides, a social worker, a chaplain, and volunteers, and it cares for the family too, with grief support after the death and short respite stays. A person can leave hospice if things change. Neither hospice nor palliative care aims to hasten death or to postpone it. The details vary with insurance and with the state, so ask your parent's own doctors what applies. Christian moral teaching, especially in the Catholic tradition, has long distinguished treatments a person ought to accept from those that may be declined because their burdens outweigh their benefits (older writers spoke of ordinary and extraordinary means), and it holds that declining such a treatment is different from intending death. Some decisions remain hard, such as a feeding tube in advanced dementia, and faithful Christians differ on them; they belong with the doctors, the family, the patient's own wishes, and a pastor.

Paul wrote 2 Corinthians as a bruised apostle, "hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair" (2 Corinthians 4:8). His hope was not that the body doesn't matter but that "the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus" (2 Corinthians 4:14). So he wrote, "Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). Anyone beside a dying parent watches the outer self waste away, and Paul does not deny it; a few lines later he admits that "we groan under our burdens" (2 Corinthians 5:4).

Then comes the death, and the grief after it. Paul told the Thessalonians he did not want them to "grieve like the rest, who are without hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). He did not tell them not to grieve. Augustine, whose mother Monica died at Ostia in 387 with him at her side, wrote in his Confessions that he held back his tears through her burial, then wept for her alone, and asked not to be scorned for weeping a little while for the mother who had wept for him for years. And if you were not there at the last moment, because you stepped out or fell asleep after nights of watching, hear what Jesus said to friends who could not stay awake in Gethsemane: "the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" (Matthew 26:41). They failed him that night, and he went on loving them.

Death is still "the last enemy to be destroyed" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and the church does the dying no favors when it pretends otherwise or hides death away in euphemism and silence, as many of us have. But the enemy is defeated, and Christians may sit beside a dying parent without lying and grieve afterward without despair. God promised his people, "Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray" (Isaiah 46:4), and into the hands of that God we commend our parents when they go through a door we cannot go through with them. One day someone will sit beside us.

scriptureStudy.note: "Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails" (Psalm 71:9). The prayer names the fear of being set aside, and it ends with "Hurry, O my God, to help me" (Psalm 71:12), the cry of someone who still expects God to come.

"Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation" (Psalm 71:18). The old still have a calling, and a hope: "You will revive me once again" (Psalm 71:20).

"When Jacob had finished instructing his sons, he pulled his feet into the bed and breathed his last" (Genesis 49:33). Then "Joseph fell upon his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him" (Genesis 50:1). Wishes spoken and honored, and a son's grief not hidden.

"Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day" (2 Corinthians 4:16). The courage rests on the resurrection named two verses earlier (2 Corinthians 4:14), not on denying that the body fails.

"Stay here and keep watch with Me" (Matthew 26:38). Jesus asked his friends to stay awake with him, and they fell asleep. He named it, and said, "the spirit is willing, but the body is weak" (Matthew 26:41). Watchers at a deathbed get tired too.

sessions.goingDeeper:
Take up the church's long practice of dying well, which many modern families have lost. In the fifteenth century, after waves of plague, short books on the art of dying, known by the Latin name ars moriendi, circulated widely in Europe, preparing the dying and those who sat with them for the temptations of the last hours, despair among them, and for a death commended into God's hands. Tolstoy pictured the opposite in The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886): a man dying amid pretense.

In 1967 Cicely Saunders, a nurse, social worker, and physician whose Christian faith shaped her work, opened St Christopher's Hospice in London, from which the modern hospice movement grew. She taught that the dying suffer pain of body, mind, relationships, and spirit, and that all of it deserves care. In 1969 Elisabeth Kübler-Ross published On Death and Dying, built on her conversations with dying patients. The five stages she described there came from the dying, not the bereaved, and they are not a required sequence for anyone's grief. A serious group should ask what it would take to recover the older wisdom: a church that visits the dying and stays, teaches its people to name their wishes before a crisis, and keeps visiting the grieving after the casseroles stop.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group has cared for her mother through six years of dementia. Hospice was called a month ago; her mother now eats very little and sleeps most of the day. The woman's brother arrives from another state, is shaken by how far their mother has declined, and wants a feeding tube, a hospital, another opinion. The woman tells the group she feels something close to relief that the long goodbye is ending, that she hates herself for it, and that her brother has accused her of giving up.

Don't take a side in a family's medical decision. Say plainly that the group can't give medical advice, and that feeding near the end of dementia is a question on which faithful Christians differ. Encourage the family to meet with the hospice team, the doctor, and their pastor, and to ask what their mother said she wanted. Help the room see that the brother may be beginning a grief his sister has lived for years, and that his request may also come from a conviction faithful Christians hold, so neither sibling is the problem. Tell her that relief after a long illness is not betrayal.

memoryVerse.text: Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.

leaderPrimer:
Your room may hold a daughter who has cared for her mother every day for five years and a son three states away who feels like a fraud, a husband caring for a wife who no longer knows his name, someone whose parent died last month, someone trying to honor a father who was cruel, and an older member who fears becoming a burden to their own children. Most have been given advice by people who have never done this. Resist the urge to fix. Keep the room safe and honest, keep pointing at the text, and protect people's decisions from the judgment of others.

Caregivers often can't come unless someone stays with the person they care for, so ask your church whether volunteers could sit with a parent or spouse during sessions. Start and end on time, let people keep their phones on, and let them leave without explanation. Each session stands on its own.

Say plainly that nothing in this study is medical, legal, or financial advice, and that you are not a doctor, a lawyer, or a counselor. Know where help is before anyone asks. The care page at /help/caregiving gathers the first steps and the calls that open doors, the eight-week plan at /plans/caregiving can carry someone between sessions, the Find Help page at /help lists the help lines, and /help/grief is there after a death.

Never ask anyone to disclose danger, abuse, or thoughts of suicide in the group. When it comes out anyway, stop, thank them, talk with them privately as soon as you can, and connect them to help. If anyone speaks of not wanting to live, of suicide, or of everyone being better off without them, take it seriously every time: stay with them and call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, together, and call 911 in immediate danger. If a caregiver fears they might hurt the person they care for, or already has, make sure that person is safe, help the caregiver step away, and call or text 988 with them now; they don't have to be suicidal to call. Then help them find respite.

Elder abuse and neglect happen, and family members are among those who commit them. If you learn that someone is hurting, neglecting, or taking money from an older adult, report it to adult protective services in the state where the older adult lives, and call 911 in immediate danger; in a nursing home or assisted living, the state's long-term care ombudsman also advocates for residents. Don't confront anyone or investigate. If anyone is afraid of someone at home, whether a spouse, an adult child, or a parent whose illness has made them aggressive, safety comes first, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788, can help them plan. Someone who was sexually abused, whenever it happened, can call the RAINN National Sexual Assault Hotline at 800-656-4673. Never counsel anyone to stay in danger to care for a parent or keep a family together. Church leaders may be mandated reporters of child abuse and, in some states, of the abuse of older or vulnerable adults; the laws vary by state, so learn your obligations before the study begins.

Caregiver exhaustion and depression are real. Watch for people who have stopped sleeping or eating, can't stop crying, feel nothing at all, or are drinking more to get through. Don't diagnose anyone; encourage them to see their own doctor and a licensed counselor. Set the rule of confidentiality at the first meeting, and state its limits as plainly: if someone is in danger, or an older adult or a child is being harmed, you will not keep that secret. Never press someone estranged from a parent to explain why.

Some questions in this study are open among faithful Christians, and the guide leaves them open. On whether honor leans toward caring for a parent at home, some say yes as long as it can be done, since children are to "repay their parents" (1 Timothy 5:4), with the comfort that costly daily presence is seen by God; others say a good facility chosen with care and visited faithfully can be honor, since a task "too heavy for you" should be shared (Exodus 18:18), with the comfort that a painful decision is not a sinful one. On telling a parent with dementia a painful truth again and again, some hold that the truth is still owed, gently, since each of us is to "speak truthfully to his neighbor" (Ephesians 4:25), with the comfort of a clear conscience; others hold that entering a confused parent's world to spare fresh grief is not the lie Scripture forbids, since "Love does no wrong to its neighbor" (Romans 13:10), with the comfort of sparing a parent fresh grief every evening. On some decisions at the end of life, such as a feeding tube in advanced dementia, some hold that food and water, even by tube, are basic care rather than medical treatment, owed to everyone whose body can still receive them (Matthew 25:35), with the comfort that no one was abandoned; others hold that a feeding tube is a treatment that may be declined when it adds burden without benefit, since there is "a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:2), with the comfort that a family can let a parent die in peace. Each side shares a floor: no abandonment, no deceiving a parent for gain, no intending death. Faithful churches differ on these questions, and James Bell's own landing is not given here. State each position fairly, and let people disagree and remain brothers and sisters.

Finally, lead from inside: many of us have watched someone carry this and offered too little. If you are a caregiver yourself, ask a co-leader to share the room and the follow-up. Five sessions will not make anyone's parent well. They can end the isolation, give tired people bread and company, and point the room, yourself first, to the God who carries his people to old age and gray hair.

faq.q: Is it wrong to move my parent into a nursing home or memory care?
faq.a: Scripture commands honor and provision and never names the place, and faithful Christians weigh this differently. Some believe honor leans toward caring for a parent at home as long as it can be done, since children are told to "repay their parents" (1 Timothy 5:4), and daily, costly presence is a gift no one else can give. Others believe that when a parent's needs outgrow what a family can safely give, a good facility, chosen with care and visited faithfully, is one way to provide, and that a task "too heavy for you" should be shared (Exodus 18:18). Both agree that abandonment is never honor and that safety comes first.

faq.q: Is it a sin to resent caring for my parent, or to wish it were over?
faq.a: Feeling resentful isn't automatically sin; it is often a warning that the load is too heavy or that someone isn't helping. The letter to the Ephesians says, "Be angry, yet do not sin. Do not let the sun set upon your anger" (Ephesians 4:26). The danger is in keeping it: contempt, taking it out on your parent, or quietly withdrawing care. A weary wish for suffering to end is not a wish to do harm. But if your thoughts turn toward hurting your parent or yourself, make sure everyone is safe, step away, and call or text 988 now.

faq.q: Do I have to take care of a parent who abused or abandoned me?
faq.a: Honoring a parent never means putting yourself back within reach of harm. If your parent is still dangerous to you, get safe first: call 911 in an emergency, and the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788) can help you plan. The command to honor has no exception written into it, but it doesn't require trust, closeness, or pretending the past didn't happen, and forgiving someone is not the same as making yourself available to them. Some give care with firm limits; others arrange care through someone else and check on it from a distance. A counselor who understands abuse can help you decide.

faq.q: My mother doesn't recognize me anymore. Is she still there? Is she still a Christian if she can't remember her faith?
faq.a: She is still your mother, and still a person made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), even when her memory can't hold who she is. Her standing before God never rested on her memory. When Zion complained that the Lord had forgotten her, God answered by imagining a mother forgetting her own child: "Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!" (Isaiah 49:15). A trustworthy saying in 2 Timothy, a letter in Paul's name, ends by resting on God's faithfulness rather than ours: "if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself" (2 Timothy 2:13). Losing a memory is not the same as denying Christ. Your visit may be gone from her mind by supper and still have been a mercy at lunch. You're allowed to miss her while she's in the room.

faq.q: What is the difference between hospice and palliative care? Does choosing hospice mean giving up?
faq.a: In general terms, palliative care relieves the pain, symptoms, and stress of a serious illness at any stage, alongside treatment meant to cure. Hospice is palliative care near the end of life; in the United States it is generally offered when a doctor expects death in six months or less if the illness runs its usual course, and the person chooses comfort over cure. A team cares for patient and family, and a person can leave hospice if things change. Neither aims to hasten death or to postpone it, and choosing hospice is not giving up on God. This is not medical or legal advice; ask your parent's own doctors what applies.

faq.q: Is it wrong to stop a treatment, or to decline a feeding tube?
faq.a: Christian moral teaching, especially in the Catholic tradition, has long held that a person need not accept every possible treatment, especially one whose burdens outweigh its benefits near the end, and that declining it is different from intending death. On some decisions faithful Christians differ. Some hold that food and water, even given by tube, are basic care rather than medical treatment, owed to everyone whose body can still receive them, remembering the Lord who said, "I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat" (Matthew 25:35). Others hold that a feeding tube is a medical treatment that may be declined when it adds burden without benefit to someone who is dying, since there is "a time to be born and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:2). Both agree that intending death is wrong and that comfort and presence are owed to the end. Talk with the doctors and your pastor, and honor your parent's known wishes. This is not medical or legal advice.

faq.q: What if I'm afraid I might hurt my parent, or someone else is hurting them?
faq.a: If you are afraid you might hurt your parent, or you already have, make sure your parent is safe, step away, and call or text 988 now; you don't have to be suicidal to call. Then tell your doctor or a counselor, and arrange respite. If someone else is hurting, neglecting, or taking money from your parent, report it to adult protective services in your parent's state, and call 911 if anyone is in danger; in a facility, the state's long-term care ombudsman also advocates for residents. You don't need to be certain to make a report.

faq.q: I'm not religious. Isn't honor just a way to guilt people into unpaid care?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and churches have earned some of it; duty preached without help has crushed people. This study refuses that version: rest is commanded beside honor, the load belongs to a family and a church rather than one person, and no one is required to stand within reach of a parent who harms them. What it adds is a claim you can weigh: that a person's worth doesn't rest on usefulness or memory, because every person bears the image of God, which protects both the parent who can no longer give anything back and the caregiver who is a creature with limits.

timeline.date: Fifteenth or thirteenth century BC (the date is debated)
timeline.event: At Sinai, God gives Israel the Ten Commandments; the command to honor father and mother comes directly after the command to keep the Sabbath (Exodus 20:8-12).
The setting of the book of Ruth, in the days when the judges ruled, where a widow from Moab binds herself to her widowed mother-in-law. The book itself was written later.
Before he becomes king, around 1010 BC, David, a fugitive from Saul, leaves his father and mother in the care of the king of Moab (1 Samuel 22:3-4).
In the reign of Ahab, the prophet Elijah flees from Jezebel and asks to die under a broom tree; God answers with sleep, food, and a companion (1 Kings 19).
At the cross, Jesus gives his mother into the keeping of the disciple he loved (John 19:25-27).
Monica dies at Ostia with her son Augustine at her side; he describes her death and his grief in the ninth book of his Confessions, written about a decade later.
Benedict of Nursia writes his Rule, which puts the care of the sick before everything else, as service to Christ, and asks for kindly consideration toward the old (chapters 36 and 37).
The first Book of Common Prayer, prepared under Thomas Cranmer, includes a marriage vow, adapted from older English rites, that promises love in sickness and in health until death.
The German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer describes a woman in her fifties with severe memory loss, and the changes he found in her brain after her death; the disease later takes his name.
Congress passes the Older Americans Act, whose later amendments establish local agencies on aging, and creates Medicare and Medicaid.
Cicely Saunders, a nurse, social worker, and physician whose Christian faith shaped her work, opens St Christopher's Hospice in London, from which the modern hospice movement grew.
Congress creates a Medicare hospice benefit, which takes effect the following year; among other things, it covers short respite stays so that a family caregiver can rest.
The Family and Medical Leave Act gives eligible employees of covered employers unpaid, job-protected leave to care for a spouse or parent with a serious health condition, though not a parent-in-law.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for coming, especially if you had to arrange care for someone at home to be here. What is said here stays here, with one exception: if someone is in danger of harming themselves or someone else, or an older adult or a child is being harmed, I will not keep that secret, and I may be required to get help. No one has to share anything, and if your phone rings, step out. This group can't give medical, legal, or financial advice. If you are ever afraid you might hurt the person you care for, or you have thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 any time; you don't have to be suicidal to call. And none of us stands above this. Some of us are caring for someone now, some have done it, and all of us will grow old if we are given the years. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, into the places where this is lived: the kitchen table covered with pill bottles, the waiting room, the drive home from the nursing home, the night you lie awake listening for footsteps in the hall.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, even though nothing is finished; caregiving is never finished in an evening. If something tonight told you that you need help, a doctor for yourself, a counselor, a few hours of respite, hear that as God's kindness and not as failure, and talk with me afterward if you'd like help finding it. If someone is harming the person you care for, or you are afraid of what you might do, tell me, call or text 988, and call 911 if anyone is in danger. Let me pray for us, and for the people we left at home tonight.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Set the ground rules on confidentiality and its limits, say that the group gives no medical, legal, or financial advice, name 988, 911, and adult protective services, and ask what would help people attend.
Week 2: Session 1, Honor in a New Season.
Week 3: Session 2, The Weariness No One Sees, with time for each person to name one specific request they will make.
Week 4: Session 3, When Roles Reverse, with extended time on the book of Ruth.
Week 5: Session 4, Hard Choices, part one: where a parent will live, money, and siblings.
Week 6: Session 4, part two: honoring a parent who was not a good parent, and safety.
Week 7: Session 5, Dying Well and Grieving.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit each session's quiet-room question, then help each person leave with one name to call for help and one specific request to make of someone who could take a shift.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, with the ground rules and safety facts set at the start.
Week 4: Session 5, Dying Well and Grieving.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Honor in a New Season.
Week 2: Session 2, The Weariness No One Sees.
Week 5: Session 5, Dying Well and Grieving.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Written about 397 to 400. The ninth book tells of the death of Augustine's mother, Monica, at Ostia in 387, her request to be remembered at the Lord's altar, and her son's grief, held back at the burial and then let go. Session 5.

bibliography.title: The Rule of Saint Benedict
bibliography.author: Benedict of Nursia
bibliography.note: A sixth-century rule for monks. Chapter 36 puts the care of the sick above everything, as service to Christ, asks the sick not to burden those who serve them, and asks the servers to bear patiently with the sick; chapter 37 asks that the weakness of the old and the young always be taken into account, with kindly consideration, especially at meals. Sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Written in 1938 and published in 1939. Its chapter on ministry calls the law of Christ in Galatians 6:2 a law of bearing, and argues that others become our brothers and sisters precisely as burdens we bear. Session 2.

bibliography.title: Habits of the Heart: Individualism and Commitment in American Life
bibliography.author: Robert N. Bellah, Richard Madsen, William M. Sullivan, Ann Swidler, and Steven M. Tipton
bibliography.note: Published in 1985. The authors argue from interviews that individualism is the first language of American moral life, with the biblical and civic traditions as second languages, and that it struggles to speak of lasting commitment. Session 1.

bibliography.title: Dependent Rational Animals: Why Human Beings Need the Virtues
bibliography.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
bibliography.note: Published in 1999. A philosopher argues that vulnerability and dependence belong to every human life, and that we need the virtues of acknowledged dependence, both giving and receiving care. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: The 36-Hour Day
bibliography.author: Nancy L. Mace and Peter V. Rabins
bibliography.note: First published in 1981 and revised many times since. A practical guide for families caring for someone with Alzheimer's disease or another dementia, including the caregiver's own needs. Not a Christian book; a practical companion for sessions 2 to 4.

bibliography.title: Being Mortal: Medicine and What Matters in the End
bibliography.author: Atul Gawande
bibliography.note: Published in 2014. A surgeon argues that medicine has often treated aging and dying as problems to fix, and commends hospice and honest conversations about what a person wants most at the end. A secular source; session 5.

bibliography.title: On Death and Dying
bibliography.author: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross
bibliography.note: Published in 1969. Built on her conversations with dying patients, it describes five stages she observed in the dying and pleads for listening to them. The stages were described for the dying, not for grief, and they are not a required sequence for anyone who grieves. Session 5.

bibliography.title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
bibliography.author: Leo Tolstoy
bibliography.note: A novella published in 1886, in which a dying judge is tormented by the pretense that he is merely ill and comforted most by a young servant who cares for him plainly and does not lie. Session 5.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Published in 1961 under a pseudonym, from the notebooks Lewis kept after his wife, Joy Davidman, died of cancer in 1960; an honest record of grief, anger at God, and a slow return. Session 5.

furtherReading: The 36-Hour Day, Nancy L. Mace and Peter V. Rabins, for practical help caring for someone with dementia.
Being Mortal, Atul Gawande, for understanding hospice and the conversations that matter at the end.
Life Together, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for churches that want to become communities that bear one another's burdens.
Confessions, Augustine, especially the ninth book, for a son's account of his mother's death and his grief.
A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for the grief after the death, and for permission to be honest with God in it.

glossary.definition: To treat someone as weighty; the Hebrew verb in Exodus 20:12 comes from a root meaning heavy. Honor is shown in deeds, but it is not the same as obedience or trust, and it never requires standing within reach of harm.
A gift devoted to God (Mark 7:11). The tradition Jesus condemned let a son declare his resources Corban and then refuse to support his parents.
Two words in Galatians 6: the burden of verse 2 is a heavy weight others are told to help carry; the load of verse 5 is the pack each person carries himself.
The Hebrew word often translated loving devotion: loyalty beyond what duty requires, as in Ruth's care for Naomi.
Care that gives a family caregiver a break, such as a helper at home, an adult day program, or a short stay in a care facility.
Medical care that relieves the pain, symptoms, and stress of a serious illness, at any stage and alongside treatment meant to cure.

Palliative care near the end of life for someone who has chosen comfort over cure, given at home or in a facility by a team that also supports the family. It aims neither to hasten death nor to postpone it.
Grief that begins before a death, as someone declines. It is real grief, and caregivers in long illnesses such as dementia often know it well.
A general term for a decline in memory, thinking, and judgment severe enough to interfere with daily life; Alzheimer's disease is one of its causes. Only a qualified professional can diagnose it.

A legal document naming someone to handle a person's affairs, which stays in effect if the person loses the capacity to decide. It generally must be signed while the person can still understand it; rules vary by state.
A document naming someone to make medical decisions for a person who can no longer make them, often part of an advance directive. Names and forms vary by state.
The state agency that takes and looks into reports of abuse, neglect, or exploitation of older adults and adults with disabilities.
An advocate for residents of nursing homes, assisted living, and similar facilities, found in every state.

Harm done to an older adult by someone they should be able to trust: physical, emotional, or sexual abuse, neglect, or financial exploitation. Report it to adult protective services, and call 911 in danger.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Caring for an aging parent, or for a husband or wife whose health is failing, can be some of the loneliest work in a church. This five-session study opens Scripture on honor, the weariness no one sees, the reversal of roles, the hard choices about care, money, and family, and dying well. It gives no medical, legal, or financial advice, and it never asks anyone to carry this alone. If coming means finding someone to stay with the person you care for, tell us, and we will try to help you get here.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study for caregivers called When Our Parents Grow Old. It's for anyone caring for an aging parent or for a husband or wife whose health is failing, whether every day or from three states away, and for those of us who want to learn to help. It won't tell anyone what to do with their parents, and it won't pile on guilt. If you can't come because you can't leave someone alone, talk to me, and we'll try to help you get here.
promoKit.inviteCaption: "Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray" (Isaiah 46:4). A five-session study for those caring for an aging parent or an ailing husband or wife. Honest about the weariness, and no one carrying it alone.
quoteCards: The God who told you to honor your father and mother also told you to stop.
When Elijah had nothing left, God didn't send a lecture. He sent bread, and then he sent it again.
Your exhaustion isn't a verdict on your love. It may be a sign that you're carrying what was meant for many.
Love changes its shape when a parent grows old. It doesn't change its object.
Arranging care through other hands is not the same as walking away.
Death is still an enemy. It is not the last word.
